narrative:
The model estimated a 65.9% probability that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means roughly a two-in-three chance of failure and a one-in-three chance of passing; it is not a certainty, but it was high enough to lead to rejection.

The decisive factor was your third-year class standing. You are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. This was the strongest push toward a fail prediction. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, below the accepted average of 3.23, was the second-most influential item, but it worked in your favor and slightly offset the risk. Your first-year class standing, also in the lowest decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, was third-most influential and pushed toward failure. The denial was therefore driven mainly by persistently low class rankings. Gender and race were not used.

To improve future chances, ask admissions for feedback, take structured bar-prep and analytical-writing coursework, consider post-baccalaureate work to strengthen your academic record, and consider retaking the LSAT (32 versus an accepted average of 37.18). Reapply after showing clear improvement and a credible plan for first-time bar success.
